title: Time and Order
theme: The roots chron and temp: time
objectives: I can use the roots chron and temp, both meaning time, to work out the meaning of ten words.
I can sort words by whether their time root is Greek (chron) or Latin (temp).
I can use the prefixes syn-, ana-, con-, and ex- and the suffixes -ic, -ical, -ize, -ism, -ary, and -al to explain how a word is built.
I can write about order and timing in a story or an exhibit using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: Two roots that both mean time give students a rare chance to see how English borrows from two languages for one idea. Chron comes from Greek and tempor from Latin, so the ten words sort cleanly into two families, and within each family the affixes show whether a word names length (chronic, temporary), sequence (chronological, chronicle), sameness (synchronize, contemporary), mismatch (anachronism), speed (tempo), or a speaker's lack of preparation (extemporaneous). The passage uses a museum exhibit so that sequence and timing are concrete. These words are common in history, music, science and literature, and they reward the habit of breaking an unfamiliar word into its parts.

words.def: To make things happen at the same time or at the same speed.

words.def: Belonging to the present time; modern.

senses.def: Belonging to the same period as another person or event.
senses.example: Mozart and Haydn were contemporary composers, because their lifetimes overlapped.

words.ex: The gallery shows contemporary artists who are working right now.
words.ex2: The museum's contemporary wing displays work made in the last few years.
words.nonExample: A statue from ancient Greece is not contemporary art.

morph.note: With plus time: of the same time.

passage.title: The Six-Week Exhibit
paras: The Millbrook Museum's new exhibit was temporary, scheduled to run for only six weeks, and the eighth-grade curators had one job: arrange the town's history in chronological order. Their guide, Mr. Idowu, handed each student a box of photographs, letters, and tickets. “A chronicle only works if the sequence is right,” he said. “Put one thing in the wrong decade and the whole story wobbles.”

Lila found the first problem. A photograph labeled 1902 showed a woman carrying a plastic shopping bag, an obvious anachronism, since plastic bags did not exist then. The label was wrong. Meanwhile, Omar was wrestling with a chronic problem of his own: the museum's two hall clocks had disagreed for years. “Let's synchronize them,” Mr. Idowu said, and the students set both to the same minute so that every caption on the timeline would match.

As the days passed, the work found its own tempo: sort in the morning, label after lunch, double-check before closing. Mr. Idowu taught them to read the temporal clues in each object, such as a date stamp, a price, or a style of clothing. The curators also wanted a contemporary section about the town as it is now, so Priya photographed the new skate park and the farmers market. “History is not only the past,” she said. “It is what is happening beside us.”

On opening night, the museum director asked one student to say a few words. Dev had no script, so he gave an extemporaneous speech. “I thought history was just dates,” he said. “But it is also people who tried to keep track of time and tell the story in order.” The audience applauded, and Mr. Idowu smiled at the clocks, which now showed the same time.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word “anachronism” most nearly means
choices: a spelling mistake in a caption
a photograph that has faded over time
an object that is very old
something that appears in the wrong time period
qs.why: A plastic bag in a photograph labeled 1902 is an item that did not exist then, so it belongs to a later time than the label claims.

qs.q: Why does Mr. Idowu have the students synchronize the two hall clocks?
choices: So the times on the timeline captions will match.
Because the clocks were broken and could not be fixed.
Because the museum wanted to display the clocks as antiques.
Because Dev planned to time his speech.
qs.why: The students set both clocks to the same minute so that every caption on the timeline would match.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the exhibit was temporary?
choices: It was arranged in chronological order.
It was scheduled to run for only six weeks.
It included a contemporary section on the town today.
Mr. Idowu gave each student a box of objects.
qs.why: Temporary means lasting for a short time, and the opening sentence says the exhibit would run for only six weeks.

qs.q: Dev's speech was called “extemporaneous” because it
choices: listed every date in order
was recorded for the museum
was made up without a script
was written by Mr. Idowu
qs.why: The passage says Dev had no script, so he spoke on the spot.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Telling history well means keeping events in the right order and noticing that the present is becoming the past.
Museums should never display modern objects.
Clocks are the most important objects in any exhibit.
Students cannot be trusted to label historical photographs.
qs.why: The curators work to get the order right, and Priya and Dev show that the present and the people who record time are part of history.

teacher.overview: Students use two roots meaning time, Greek chron and Latin tempor, to build and sort ten words, and then use the words to talk about length, order, timing and speed. The unit gives a second year of prefix and suffix work, and the museum narrative makes sequence concrete. It supports the history and literature units that ask students to arrange events and detect details that do not belong to a period.

notes.va.chronic.adj: Chronic means lasting a long time or recurring; it does not mean severe or terrible. Ask students to sort problems into chronic and temporary. Use chron plus -ic as the model for a word built from a root and a suffix.
notes.va.chronicle.n: Chronicle is a noun for a record in time order and also a verb (to chronicle). It comes from the same family as chron, which is worth pointing out. Distinguish it from a story: a chronicle follows time, and a narrative has a point of view and a plot.
notes.va.chronological.adj: Chronological is the key everyday word of the family. Practice with scrambled events that students put in chronological order. Show that a linking o joins chron and log. Note the noun chronology and the adverb chronologically.
notes.va.synchronize.v: Synchronize is syn- (together) plus chron (time) plus -ize (to make). Demonstrate it: two groups clap a pattern, first apart, then synchronized. Students often confuse it with synonym because of the shared prefix syn-.
notes.va.anachronism.n: Anachronism is a high-interest word: students enjoy finding a wristwatch on a Roman soldier. Remind them that an anachronism is out of its time, not simply old or new. Check that students can say what the object is and which period it does not belong to.
notes.va.tempo.n: Tempo is Italian for time, borrowed by English through music. Connect to the sense of pace in a story or a game. Ask students to read a sentence at a slow and at a fast tempo and say what changes.
notes.va.temporary.adj: Temporary pairs with permanent. Students often spell it temperary or confuse it with temper. Use the root tempor to link it to temporal and contemporary. Ask students for a temporary fix that became permanent.
notes.va.temporal.adj: Temporal means having to do with time. It is the time version of spatial. Use it with timelines and sequences. The word also has other uses (for example, the temporal bone of the skull), which can be mentioned if students meet it.
notes.va.contemporary.adj: Contemporary has two senses: modern, and from the same time. The unit teaches modern as the main sense and shows the second sense so students can read both in history texts. Ask which sense fits each sentence. The parts are con- (with) plus tempor (time).
notes.va.extemporaneous.adj: Extemporaneous means made up without preparation. Students may confuse it with temporary because of the shared root. The parts ex (out of) plus tempor (time) are a clue to the phrase out of the moment. In speech contests the word can mean delivered from notes, so check the context.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The label says 1902 but the photo shows a plastic bag. I see temporal clues that do not match, so I will call it an anachronism. The root chron means time, so chronological means in time order. I need to arrange the exhibit that way, and I should synchronize the clocks so the captions match.”

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: crónico, crónica, cronológico, sincronizar, anacronismo, tempo/ritmo, temporal/provisional (temporary), temporal (Spanish also means storm), contemporáneo, improvisado (extemporaneous).

Morphology: chronological uses a linking o respelled in the note (chron -> chrono); anachronism segment ana- is glossed as back/against and the note says only that the pieces suggest something set against its proper time; extemporaneous, tempo and chronicle are not segmented because the final pieces are not standard English affixes or are borrowed whole.
Teacher notes state that tempo is Italian for time and that chronicle belongs to the chron family and that the extemporaneous parts are ex plus tempor; confirm against a dictionary.
Sense boundaries: chronicle (noun taught, verb as a second sense); contemporary (modern taught, same-period sense as a second sense); temporal (time sense only).
Fact: plastic shopping bags did not exist in 1902; Mozart and Haydn lifetimes overlapped.
